name: Pioneer 10
significance: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft sent to the outer Solar System, and nobody knew whether it would survive the trip. Between July 1972 and February 1973 it became the first craft to cross the asteroid belt, which some had feared would be a shooting gallery of debris; it was hit far less than expected. In December 1973 it became the first to fly past Jupiter, returning the first close-up pictures of the planet and its Great Red Spot and photographing the moons Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. It found that Jupiter's radiation belts were far more intense than expected, strong enough to trigger false commands on board, and that the planet is mostly liquid. Those radiation maps shaped the design of every later Jupiter mission. Jupiter's gravity then flung it out of the Solar System: in June 1983 it crossed the orbit of Neptune, then the most distant planet, the first human-made object to go beyond the planets. It carries a gold plaque, designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake, showing who sent it and from where.
statusNote: Launched 1972-03-03 01:49 UTC (8:49 p.m. EST on 2 March, the date NASA gives; Siddiqi's Beyond Earth prints “2 March 1972 / 01:49:04 UT”, pairing the US date with the UT time; NSSDCA 1972-012A and Horizons give 3 March, Horizons at 01:49:00) on an Atlas-Centaur from Cape Kennedy. Entered the asteroid belt 1972-07-15 and left it in February 1973 (Siddiqi; NASA release 03-082). Jupiter closest approach 1973-12-04 02:26 UT at 130,354 km above the cloud tops (Siddiqi; NASA gives 3 December, the US date); Horizons puts it at 02:25, 203,123 km from Jupiter's centre (about 131,600 km above the cloud tops; its header says "approximately 2.8 Jovian radii (about 200,000 km)"). Crossed Saturn's orbit in February 1976 and the orbit of Neptune, then the outermost planet, on 1983-06-13 (Siddiqi; NASA's 2003 release says it passed Pluto's orbit in 1983). Routine science ended 1997-03-31; last telemetry 2002-04-27; last, very weak signal 2003-01-22 (NASA release 03-082; Siddiqi says 23 January). TRAJECTORY: JPL Horizons -23, "provided by JPL Navigation Team" from source files PN10A-G and the DE118 planetary ephemeris; Horizons notes "the circumstances pertaining to the regeneration of the above spacecraft trajectory source files PN10* are not well known" and that it is "suitable for general historical purposes, but should be used cautiously for high precision". Horizons is the primary source here, so the path is drawn solid: Lambert legs between real Horizons positions, with a Jupiter tour in the planet view (tools/build_voyager.py, tools/build_planet_tour.py). The path stops where Pioneer 10 passes 54.514 AU from the Sun, 1.1 x Pluto's farthest distance, the edge of the Solar System view until the heliosphere layer exists (docs/outer-missions-plan.md section 1). Moon distances: closest approaches computed from Horizons (tools/moon_passes.py).

legs._comment: Heliocentric path built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_voyager.py from JPL Horizons (target -23): Lambert legs between real positions; planet tours spliced in; ends where the craft passes 54.514 AU (1.1 x Pluto's aphelion), the edge of the Solar System view for now.

Jupiter tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -23, 1973-12-01 -> 1973-12-08): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.
1992-06-07: crosses 54.514 AU from the Sun (Horizons, hourly); the path stops here until the heliosphere layer exists.
